title_zh: 没有上级，约定为什么还算数？
deck_zh: 一个小国等了五个月，一份流域协议没有签成，一条旧的通报义务却还在。合作不是大家时时点头，而是分清：究竟已经答应了什么。
deck_en: An applicant waits five months. A new river agreement fails. An older duty to give warning remains. Cooperation starts by distinguishing what has been accepted from what has not.
body_zh: 石峡邦申请加入的时候，另外三个国家中，两个很快同意了，一个没有。石峡邦便等了五个月。
先不急着把这五个月叫作程序失灵。在这个虚构故事里，各国原先约定，接纳新成员必须获得全体书面同意。若秘书长可以说“已经等得够久，算你同意”，那份全体同意便只在没人反对时才是真的。
等待当然不是没有代价。石峡邦控制着镜海通往外洋的唯一海路，人口只有一千一百万。体系外的高原联邦不希望它加入；它约七成燃料从那里进口，三家银行又收到要被审查结算的信。它不能等到各国讲完道理，才开始承受这些压力。
迟迟没有给出同意的是 DRP，也就是目的民主共和国。那年夏天，它与高原联邦签了一份便宜的化肥长约。有议员说，两件事没有关系；也有人说，时间不像巧合。原论文没有替我们判定二者之间存在什么交易，散文也不能把猜测填成内幕。
五个月后，DRP 的人民议会通过了接纳。石峡邦自己的邦议院也批准加入：一百八十席里，一百二十一票赞成，五十九票反对。它的法律要求一百二十票，刚刚多出一票。
一份看似属于“大家”的约，实际是这样经过不同的人、不同的门槛，才成立的。
## 同意，不是每天重新点头
没有共同上级的约，最容易被误解成一张心情表：今天愿意就做，明天不愿意就不做。若真是这样，谁也无法依它安排生活。
但同意一份约，也可以是同意此后按某种程序办事。各国可以先约定，哪几类事项由多数决定，哪几类必须重新取得各方同意。后来某一次表决不合自己的心意，不等于事先接受的程序突然失效。多数的效力来自那份已认下的程序，不是来自人多便自然有权。
故事里的宪约把事情分开：加入新成员、增加新的共同约束，需要全体同意；追问已经发生的事、形成记录，则不把开门的钥匙交给被问的那一方。具体多少票、怎样回避，是这里给的一种写法，不是唯一的写法。
这一区分使合作既不必变成一个总能加新要求的上级，也不至于每逢有人不高兴，便连已经约好的问都问不了。一个成员可以不同意增加一条义务，不能因此假装旧的义务从未存在。
不过，“它已同意”还要再拆一层。石峡邦的一百二十一票依当地法律足够让加入成立，五十九张反对票并没有因此变成赞成票。这是国家经自己的程序作出的同意，不是每一位居民的内心都说了同一句话。那些反对的人，此后仍能在本国的渠道里继续问这件事。
同样，石峡邦加入以后与 DRP 各有一票，说的是两国在共同安排里的地位，不是在宣称两国的每一个人得到了同样分量的政治代表。一国一票既不消灭人口差别，也不保证强者从此不再影响弱者。它在这里要守住的是：不能把市场、人口或军力直接兑成一个额外的表决位置。
申请加入也不等于请求某一个大国收留。三界镇设在 NUT，也就是目的民族联盟境内，秘书处在那里办公，驻地国却不能因此多出权限。有人提供地方，有人先发起，都可以承认；这些贡献不自动变成“所以此后由我说了算”。
## 新约没有签成，河还是会流下来
加入之后，石峡邦又遇到一份自己不愿签的约。这次不是入会，是河流。
云河从 NUT 流入 UCSE，也就是目的联合城邦，最后入海。两国早有一份关于分水与汛情通报的协定，又经仲裁确定了流量和传送数据的要求。石峡邦的峡水是云河的一条支流；石峡邦进来以后，秘书处起草了一份三方流域议定书，希望把数据和共同安排扩展过去。
石峡邦拒签。一方面，它的电站贷款合同限制向第三方提供运行数据，贷款银行不同意放行；另一方面，邦议院的水利委员会认为，新草案要求的枯水季流量在蓄水年份过高。两种理由不能揉成一个“它就是不合作”。对下游有用的安排，在上游也有代价。
没有签，三方的新约就没有成立。UCSE 与 NUT 随后另订双边补充协议，把自己能取得的数据送到秘书处的数据站。这份协议不能把石峡邦算作当事方，也不能替它承诺交出电站数据。
同一个夏天，电站闸门出了故障，紧急泄洪。石峡邦在泄洪开始四十分钟后才通知 NUT。下游两个村被淹，一人死亡。苹果城收到转来的测站数据，在洪峰到达前九小时发出了预警。
这时，再问石峡邦，就不是逼它补签那份没有成立的新约。它加入时已经接受过宪约中的通报义务：可能影响别国境内的人，事先通报；来不及，事后即刻通报。那条义务并不等三方流域议定书成立才生效。
所以新约和旧约必须分开。拒绝新的数据要求，不等于已经答应过的通报也可以不算。贷款合同管什么，同样要分开：运行数据是一件事，泄洪以后及时通知是另一件事。不能只说“合同不许”，便把没有被合同禁止的那一件一起藏进去。
入冬以后，石峡邦与 NUT 又订了泄洪前电话通报的办法。这是一个进展，却不替夏天结案。下次怎样通知，与这一次两个村被淹、一个人死去，不能合成一张已经处理完的表。
数据站也确实有用。它给苹果城留下了九个小时。但电站运行数据依然没有提供。九个小时是真实得到的东西，没有取得的数据也是真实的缺口。若只承认前者，合作就成了宣传；若只看后者，又会把已经发生的保护一笔抹掉。
## 一份约，可以替谁答应到哪里
在河上很容易看见，退出一份协议，与退出彼此的生活，不是同一件事。石峡邦不签，水还是流下来；两国不再合作，洪水也不会因此认出新的边界。越是没有一个共同上级，越要把已经答应的范围、还没有答应的部分写清楚。
但各国都同意，也不等于可以把任何东西写进约里。设想一份遣返安排要求把人交回一个会遭酷刑或无审判拘押的地方。纸上有几国的签字，并不替那些面临危险的人作出了同意，也不能让签字者对他们的责任自动减少。这是本系列提出的哲学要求，不是在这里替实际案件作法律裁判。
同理，分担接纳的安排，首先分的是各国承担的份额，不是把已经来到的人当作货物分配。不能一面说合作是为了人，一面以合作的名义把人从决定里拿走。具体怎样判断风险、怎样安排去处，需要相应的法律与实际判断，不由一句原则代办。
于是，一份约每多管一件事，都值得再问：它解决哪个问题，为什么要共同管，代价落在谁身上？这不是要求条文越少越好。洪水预警、跨境申诉、公开记录都可能需要细致的程序。要少的，是没有说明必要性就添进来的权限，不是人实际需要的保障。
共同安排也可以涉及成员境内发生的事。例如，一个成员接受个人申诉程序，就已经答应在相应范围内作答。涉及内部，不自动等于接管内部；共同程序问得到，不等于共同机关从此可以替那一国治理。
成员与体系外的国家另签贸易协议，也不能仅因别的成员不喜欢，便被共同机关否决。但那项协议与履行旧约有没有冲突、是否实际压住了别人，仍可以分别问。若要增加新的共同限制，应走订立新约的路，不能拿一次临时的不满偷偷代替。
最难的地方仍然没有消失：有人可以迟迟不给新约，有些数据可以一直得不到，外面的强者也可能借会议室以外的力量施压。合作没有因为把程序分清，就能把这些困难全收走。
可它至少不必只有两个答案：要么由一个中心替所有人决定，要么所有承诺随时作废。那条河让我们看见中间的路——这一件已经答应，就照这一件作答；下一件还没答应，不能假装已经答应；后来补好了办法，也别把此前受过的损失盖过去。
约定的分量，有时就在这种不肯混在一起的耐心里。
body_en: Stonegorge waits five months for an answer. Two members of the cooperation system have accepted its application. The third has not. Nobody at the secretariat can fill in the missing consent.

This is a fictional case, not an account of a real accession dispute. The rules the three members previously accepted require unanimous written agreement for a new member. If the secretary-general could declare that everyone has waited long enough, unanimity would mean only that nobody objects until an official decides the objection has expired.

The wait is costly. Stonegorge, a country of eleven million people, controls both shores of the only passage from the Mirror Sea to the ocean. The much larger Plateau Federation opposes its application. Stonegorge imports about seventy percent of its fuel from the federation; three of its banks have received letters threatening a review of their settlement arrangements.

Meanwhile, the member withholding consent—DRP—signs a favorable long-term fertilizer contract with the federation. Some legislators deny a connection. Others question the timing. The source does not establish a bargain between the two events. An essay should not manufacture one because it would make the story simpler.

DRP eventually agrees through its assembly. Stonegorge’s own legislature votes 121 to 59 to join. Its law requires 120 votes. The compact is accepted by a margin of one vote above that threshold, not by a sudden disappearance of disagreement.
## Accepting a procedure is not agreeing with every result

An agreement without a superior enforcer can sound like a daily declaration of goodwill: we do it while we feel like doing it. Nobody could organize a dependable relationship on that basis. But accepting a compact can also mean accepting a procedure for decisions that have not yet been made.

The parties may agree that some matters will be decided by a majority. A later result then need not match every participant’s preference to count. Its authority comes from the procedure previously accepted, not from a general entitlement of the more numerous to command the rest. An unwelcome decision and a new obligation never accepted are different things.

The Three-Borders Compact distinguishes them. Adding a member or a new common obligation requires fresh agreement. Questioning existing conduct and publishing a record use a different procedure, one that does not hand the subject of a question control over whether it may be asked. The particular voting rules are examples, not the only possible institutional form.

That division prevents two opposite failures. A common body cannot keep inventing obligations merely by calling a vote. A member cannot make an old obligation disappear merely because it now dislikes being questioned. Refusing a new commitment is not the same as withdrawing every commitment already made.

There is another distinction inside the word consent. Stonegorge’s 121 votes meet its legal threshold. The 59 opposing votes have not changed sides. State consent is a decision made through a particular national procedure; it is not evidence that every person has inwardly agreed. Those who opposed accession remain people who may question it through their own institutions.

Once admitted, Stonegorge has one vote, as DRP does. This expresses the members’ institutional standing. It does not establish equal political representation for each individual across countries with different populations. Nor does one vote each prove that influence outside the room has vanished. The choice here is not to convert population, markets, or armed strength into an additional voting position.

Joining also need not mean attaching oneself to a permanent patron. Three Borders is a town in NUT, which hosts the secretariat. The headquarters agreement gives the host no additional authority. Providing a building, initiating discussions, or contributing more resources may be useful facts. None automatically becomes a standing right to decide for everyone else.
## A river does not wait for a signature

After accession, Stonegorge encounters an agreement it does not wish to sign. The Cloud River runs from NUT through UCSE to the sea. Those two countries already have an agreement on water and flood information, with an arbitration award specifying obligations. Stonegorge’s Gorgewater joins the Cloud upstream of a reservoir in NUT. The secretariat proposes extending cooperation across the basin.

The draft seeks shared operational data and a minimum dry-season flow, among other provisions. Stonegorge refuses. Its power station was financed under a contract restricting disclosure of operating data, and the lender will not consent. Its legislative water committee also considers the proposed flow too high in years when the station is filling its reservoir. Downstream benefits have upstream costs. Calling all hesitation uncooperative would hide that fact.

Without Stonegorge’s signature, the three-party protocol does not take effect. UCSE and NUT instead conclude a bilateral supplement, sharing information they can obtain themselves through a secretariat data station. Their agreement cannot turn Stonegorge into a party or promise its station’s operational records on its behalf.

That summer a gate fails at the power station. An emergency release follows. Stonegorge notifies NUT forty minutes after the release begins. Two villages downstream are flooded; one person dies. Farther downstream, Apple City receives readings relayed from a measuring station and issues a warning nine hours before the flood crest arrives.

Now there is a question for Stonegorge, but it is not a demand that the rejected protocol be signed retroactively. On joining, Stonegorge accepted an existing compact obligation: give advance notice when an action may affect people in another member’s territory, or immediate notice afterward if advance notice is impossible. That undertaking did not depend on the new basin protocol succeeding.

The distinction is essential. Stonegorge did not accept the proposed new data regime. It did accept a notification duty. A lender’s restriction on operating data does not, without more, answer a question about the timing of a warning. We need to identify which commitment applies to which act, rather than allow the largest disputed issue to swallow all the smaller ones.

In winter Stonegorge and NUT agree on advance telephone notification for releases. It is a useful improvement. It does not settle what happened that summer. Preventing the next loss and answering for the earlier loss are not interchangeable achievements.

The data station also worked. Apple City received nine hours of warning. The power station’s own operating data remained unavailable. Both belong in the account: the protection achieved and the gap that persists. Recording only the success would be publicity. Recording only the gap would erase something that helped people downstream.
## What nobody can sign away for someone else

The river makes another distinction visible. Leaving an agreement is not leaving a relationship. Water still arrives after a signature is withheld. Countries may be able to exit a particular arrangement without being able to exit one another’s effects. That is a reason for careful boundaries and dependable ways to question, not a reason to keep every compact thin.

Still, the fact that all governments agree does not make every possible term acceptable. Imagine a return agreement that would send someone to torture or detention without trial. Government signatures do not supply that person’s consent or automatically reduce the signing states’ responsibilities toward them. This is a philosophical limit advanced by the series, not a substitute judgment about the law in an actual case.

The same concern applies to sharing the costs of receiving people who have fled. States can distribute contributions and available places. That does not make the people themselves cargo to be allocated. An arrangement supposedly for people cannot justify removing those people from the question of where they will live. The practical arrangements and assessment of danger still require law and judgment; a principle cannot complete that work in advance.

Every additional common rule therefore deserves a plain explanation. What problem does it address? Why must the matter be handled jointly? Who bears the cost? This is not a demand for the shortest possible treaty. Flood warnings, cross-border petitions, and public records may require elaborate procedures. The excess to avoid is unexplained power, not useful protection.

A common undertaking may concern conduct inside a member country. A state that accepts an individual-petition procedure has accepted answering within its scope. That does not hand the common body authority to govern the country. Reaching an internal act with a question is different from taking over the decisions of internal government.

Likewise, a member’s separate trade agreement with an outside state is not subject to a common veto merely because other members dislike it. Its compatibility with commitments already accepted can still be questioned. So can pressure exerted through it. A new common restriction, if desired, must be adopted as one; disapproval of a particular deal cannot quietly do the work of an unaccepted treaty clause.

None of this eliminates the hard part. A member may continue withholding a new agreement. Important information may remain unavailable. A powerful outsider may use fuel and credit to influence decisions for which it has no vote. Institutional clarity does not dissolve those dependencies. They must remain available for a separate account.

But there are more than two options: a center empowered to decide everything, or promises that count for nothing. Between them lies the patient work of distinguishing commitments. This was accepted; answer for it. That was not accepted; do not pretend it was. A later improvement is welcome; do not let it erase the people harmed before it arrived.

Sometimes that patience is what gives an agreement its weight. Not a single signature that settles the entire relationship, but a series of commitments whose scope people can identify, rely on, and question when the river comes down.
